# Technical Brief: Database Storage and Transaction Internals

---

## 1. Write-Ahead Logging (WAL)

**Mechanism A — ARIES physiological logging with LSNs.** ARIES (Algorithms for Recovery and Isolation Exploiting Semantics, Mohan et al. 1992) assigns every log record a monotonically increasing **Log Sequence Number (LSN)**. Each page carries a **pageLSN** recording the LSN of the last update applied to it, and each log record carries a **prevLSN** chaining a transaction's records backward. Logging is **physiological**: physical with respect to the page (a redo record names a page ID), logical within the page (e.g., "insert key k in slot array"), which tolerates intra-page reorganization such as slot compaction. The **WAL protocol invariant** is that a dirty page may be flushed only after all log records up to its pageLSN are durably on stable storage (`flushedLSN ≥ pageLSN`), and a transaction commits only after its commit record is flushed.

**Mechanism B — Steal/No-Force buffer management policies.** The buffer-pool policy space is defined by two axes: **steal** (uncommitted dirty pages may be evicted/written, requiring **undo** information in the log) vs. **no-steal**, and **force** (all dirty pages flushed at commit) vs. **no-force** (requiring **redo** information). ARIES and essentially all high-performance engines choose **steal/no-force**, maximizing buffer-pool flexibility and commit latency at the cost of needing both undo and redo logging; this choice is precisely what necessitates the three-pass recovery described in §8.

**Mechanism C — Group commit.** Because commit durability requires an fsync of the log, naïve per-transaction flushing bounds throughput by storage sync latency. **Group commit** batches the commit records of many concurrent transactions into a single log flush, amortizing the fsync; the leader of a batch flushes while followers wait on the flushedLSN. PostgreSQL exposes this via `commit_delay`/`commit_siblings`; MySQL/InnoDB implements binlog group commit with ordered stages (flush → sync → commit).

**Mechanism D — Torn-page protection: doublewrite buffer and full-page writes.** Physiological redo assumes the page image on disk is internally consistent, but a crash mid-write can leave a **torn page** (partial sector write). InnoDB's **doublewrite buffer** writes each page first to a contiguous scratch area, fsyncs, then writes it to its home location; recovery can repair a torn home copy from the doublewrite area. PostgreSQL's **full_page_writes** instead logs the entire page image on the first modification after each checkpoint, so redo can restore the page wholesale rather than applying a delta to a corrupt image.

---

## 2. Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC)

**Mechanism A — PostgreSQL append-only tuple versioning (xmin/xmax + VACUUM).** Each heap tuple carries **xmin** (creating transaction ID) and **xmax** (deleting/invalidating XID). A snapshot records `xmin`, `xmax`, and the set of in-progress XIDs; **visibility rules** make a tuple visible iff its creator committed before the snapshot and its deleter (if any) did not. Updates create new tuple versions (with **HOT — Heap-Only Tuples** avoiding index churn when indexed columns are unchanged). Dead versions are reclaimed by **VACUUM**, which also prevents **XID wraparound** by freezing old tuples; the tradeoff is heap/index bloat between vacuums.

**Mechanism B — Undo-based version reconstruction (InnoDB / Oracle rollback segments).** InnoDB updates tuples **in place** and writes the before-image to **undo logs** in rollback segments; each row carries a roll pointer and trx ID. A reader with a **read view** (list of active transaction IDs at snapshot time) walks the undo chain backward, reconstructing the version visible to it. Garbage collection is the **purge** of undo records no longer needed by any read view. This yields compact heaps but makes long-running readers expensive (long undo chains; Oracle's classic "snapshot too old," ORA-01555).

**Mechanism C — Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI).** Plain **Snapshot Isolation (SI)** admits the **write-skew** anomaly (two transactions read overlapping data and write disjoint items, violating an invariant neither sees broken). **SSI** (Cahill, Röhm, Fekete 2008; PostgreSQL ≥ 9.1) tracks **rw-antidependencies** using non-blocking **SIREAD locks**; the theory shows every SI serializability violation contains a **"dangerous structure"** of two consecutive rw-antidependency edges through a pivot transaction, so SSI aborts one participant whenever such a structure forms — a conservative but low-overhead guarantee of full serializability. **Predicate/index-range SIREAD locks** close phantom gaps.

**Mechanism D — Timestamp-ordered in-memory MVCC (Hekaton / MVOCC).** Microsoft Hekaton (SQL Server In-Memory OLTP) keeps versions as latch-free linked structures with **begin/end timestamp** fields; writers install versions with their transaction ID as a tentative timestamp, and a validation phase (optimistic MVCC) re-checks read sets and commit dependencies before assigning the final commit timestamp — lock-free and latch-free on the hot path.

---

## 3. Log-Structured Merge (LSM) Trees

**Mechanism A — Memtable + SSTable architecture.** Writes go to a WAL (for durability) and an in-memory **memtable** (typically a skiplist). When full, the memtable is sealed as immutable and **flushed** as a sorted, immutable **SSTable (Sorted String Table)** with an index block and metadata; a **MANIFEST/version edit** log records the level structure atomically. Deletes are **tombstones** — logical deletion markers that mask older versions until compaction physically drops them (Cassandra retains them for `gc_grace_seconds` to prevent resurrection on replica repair).

**Mechanism B — Compaction strategies: leveled vs. size-tiered vs. universal.** **Leveled compaction** (LevelDB, RocksDB default) organizes levels L1…Ln with exponentially growing capacity and **non-overlapping key ranges within a level**; compacting an SSTable merges it with overlapping files in the next level. It minimizes **space amplification** (~1.1×) and read amplification (≤1 file per level) at the cost of high **write amplification** (~10× per level). **Size-tiered compaction (STCS**, Cassandra) merges similarly sized runs when a tier accumulates enough of them: low write amplification, but high space/read amplification since key ranges overlap across runs. RocksDB's **universal compaction** is a tiered hybrid bounding overall size ratio. The **RUM conjecture** (Read/Update/Memory) formalizes that no design minimizes all three amplifications simultaneously; **Monkey** (Dayan et al.) optimally reallocates Bloom-filter memory across levels.

**Mechanism C — Bloom filters and fence pointers.** Each SSTable carries a **Bloom filter** so point lookups skip runs that provably lack the key (false positives only, tunable bits/key); RocksDB also supports **prefix Bloom filters** for bounded-prefix seeks. **Fence pointers** (per-block min/max keys, i.e., the sparse index) let a lookup binary-search to the single 4–64 KB block to read, bounding I/O per consulted run to one block.

---

## 4. B+Tree Maintenance

**Mechanism A — Node splits, merges, and redistribution.** On overflow, a leaf **splits** at the separator key, pushing a copy of the split key into the parent; interior splits push the median up (classic B+tree). On underflow (below fill factor, typically ~50% minimum / ~70% target), a node first attempts **redistribution (borrowing)** from a sibling, else **merges** with it, deleting the separator from the parent — cascading upward and possibly shrinking tree height. Practical engines often use **suffix truncation** of separator keys and **prefix compression** within nodes; many (e.g., PostgreSQL nbtree) avoid eager merges, deferring to page deletion/vacuum.

**Mechanism B — Latch crabbing and optimistic lock coupling.** Physical consistency during traversal uses **latch coupling ("crabbing")**: acquire the child's latch before releasing the parent's; for writes, hold ancestor latches only while the child is "unsafe" (might split/merge). **Optimistic lock coupling (OLC)** (Leis et al.) replaces reader latches with **version counters**: readers proceed latch-free and validate the version after reading, restarting on conflict — dramatically better multicore scalability.

**Mechanism C — Lehman–Yao B-link trees.** The **B-link tree** adds to every node a **right-sibling pointer** and a **high key**. A split proceeds in two atomic steps (create right sibling, later post the separator to the parent), and any concurrent reader that observes a key above the node's high key simply **follows the link right**. This lets traversals hold at most one latch at a time and tolerate in-progress splits; PostgreSQL's nbtree is a Lehman–Yao variant.

**Mechanism D — Logged Structure Modification Operations (SMOs) and key-range locking.** In ARIES-style engines, splits/merges are **SMOs** executed as **nested top actions** bounded by a dummy CLR, so a crash mid-split either completes or rolls back the structural change independently of the user transaction. Logical phantom protection uses **key-range / next-key locking** (ARIES/KVL, ARIES/IM; InnoDB's next-key and gap locks), locking the gap between index entries so no phantom can be inserted into a scanned range.

---

## 5. Two-Phase Commit (2PC)

**Mechanism A — The canonical prepare/commit protocol and the blocking problem.** The **coordinator** sends PREPARE; each **participant** force-writes a *prepared* log record (making its vote durable and surrendering the unilateral right to abort) and votes YES/NO. On unanimous YES the coordinator force-writes a *commit* record — the **commit point** — then broadcasts the decision; participants write their outcome and ACK. 2PC is safe but **blocking**: if the coordinator fails after participants prepare, they hold locks **in doubt** until the coordinator recovers (a consequence of the asynchronous-failure impossibility results around non-blocking atomic commit).

**Mechanism B — Presumed abort and presumed commit.** **Presumed abort (PA)** (the R*/industry standard, in XA): absence of information at the coordinator implies abort, so abort records need not be forced, no abort ACKs are needed, and **read-only participants** reply READ-ONLY to PREPARE and drop out of phase 2 entirely. **Presumed commit (PC)** inverts the presumption to save messages on the common commit path but requires the coordinator to force-log the participant set *before* prepare, to avoid wrongly presuming commit for a transaction that never finished voting.

**Mechanism C — Three-phase commit (3PC).** Skeen's 3PC inserts a **pre-commit** phase so that no participant commits while another could still be in a state from which abort is possible; with a synchronous network and no partitions, surviving participants can elect a recovery coordinator and terminate without blocking. In practice 3PC is fragile under **network partitions** (can produce split-brain decisions), which is why it is rarely deployed.

**Mechanism D — Consensus-hardened commit: Paxos Commit and Spanner's 2PC-over-Paxos.** Gray & Lamport's **Paxos Commit** replaces each participant's vote with a Paxos instance so the decision survives coordinator failure (2PC is the degenerate case with one acceptor). **Google Spanner** layers 2PC over **Paxos-replicated groups**: both coordinator and participant state machines are themselves replicated, so a leader crash fails over within the group instead of blocking, and commit timestamps come from **TrueTime** with **commit-wait** to guarantee external consistency.

---

## 6. Logical Clocks

**Mechanism A — Lamport clocks.** A scalar counter per process: increment on each local event; on send, piggyback the counter; on receive, set `C := max(C, C_msg) + 1`. This guarantees the **clock condition**: if event *a* **happens-before** *b* (Lamport's `→` relation), then `C(a) < C(b)`. The converse fails — Lamport timestamps **cannot detect concurrency** — but totally ordering by (timestamp, process-ID) yields the canonical construction for replicated state machines and distributed mutual exclusion.

**Mechanism B — Vector clocks and version vectors.** A vector `V[1..n]`, one slot per process; entry-wise comparison gives a **partial order** that *exactly characterizes* happens-before (Fidge/Mattern): `V(a) < V(b) ⇔ a → b`, and incomparable vectors mean **concurrent** events. **Version vectors** apply this per replicated object to detect conflicting (sibling) versions, as in Dynamo/Riak; **dotted version vectors (DVVs)** add a "dot" for the latest event to correctly track causality when servers assign IDs on behalf of many clients, bounding sibling explosion.

**Mechanism C — Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC).** HLC (Kulkarni et al. 2014) combines a physical component `l` (max physical time seen) and a logical counter `c` that breaks ties when physical time hasn't advanced. HLC preserves the Lamport clock condition, stays within a bounded offset of physical time, and fits in a 64-bit timestamp. **CockroachDB** uses HLCs for MVCC timestamps and causality propagation across sessions; YugabyteDB and MongoDB's cluster time are similar.

**Mechanism D — TrueTime (bounded-uncertainty physical time).** Spanner's **TrueTime** API returns an interval `[earliest, latest]` guaranteed to contain real time, backed by GPS and atomic clocks. **Commit-wait** — a leader waits out the uncertainty `ε` before releasing a commit — turns bounded clock error into **external consistency (linearizable commit order)**, the physical-time dual of logical-clock causality tracking.

---

## 7. Quorum Systems

**Mechanism A — Read/write majority quorums (R + W > N) and Dynamo-style sloppy quorums.** With N replicas, requiring read quorum R and write quorum W such that **R + W > N** guarantees every read quorum intersects the latest write quorum (and **W + W > N** prevents conflicting concurrent writes); versions are discriminated by timestamps or version vectors. Dynamo/Cassandra/Riak add **sloppy quorums** with **hinted handoff** — writes accepted by *any* W healthy nodes (possibly outside the home preference list), with hints replayed to home replicas later — trading strict intersection for availability, repaired via **read repair** and **anti-entropy with Merkle trees**.

**Mechanism B — Weighted voting (Gifford 1979).** Each replica holds a number of **votes**; operations must gather read/write vote thresholds with `r + w > total votes`. This generalizes majorities: a fast or reliable replica can carry more weight, a zero-vote replica is a pure read cache, and configurations can tune read-vs-write latency. It is the historical root of quorum consensus replication.

**Mechanism C — Grid and tree quorums.** Arranging N nodes in a √N×√N **grid**, a quorum can be one full row plus one element from every row (or row+column variants): quorum size O(√N) instead of O(N/2), with every pair of quorums still intersecting. Tree quorum protocols (Agrawal–El Abbadi) achieve O(log N) quorums in the failure-free case. These illustrate the general theory: a quorum system is any intersecting set system, trading **load, capacity, and availability** (Naor–Wool).

**Mechanism D — Flexible Paxos (FPaxos).** Howard et al. proved Paxos does not need all quorums to be majorities: only **phase-1 (leader election) quorums Q1 and phase-2 (replication) quorums Q2 must intersect each other** (|Q1| + |Q2| > N), not Q2 with Q2. Thus a steady-state leader can commit with a small Q2 (fast, available for writes) at the cost of a large Q1 on failover — directly exploited in modern Raft/Paxos deployments and in Heidi Howard's generalized quorum-intersection framework.

---

## 8. Crash Recovery

**Mechanism A — ARIES three-pass recovery.** (1) **Analysis** scans forward from the last checkpoint rebuilding the **Dirty Page Table (DPT)** (page → recLSN, first LSN that may have dirtied it) and the **Transaction Table (ATT)** (status, lastLSN) to determine losers and the redo start point (min recLSN). (2) **Redo** implements **"repeating history"**: every logged action — including those of loser transactions — is reapplied if `pageLSN < LSN of the record`, restoring the exact pre-crash state; the pageLSN test makes redo **idempotent**. (3) **Undo** rolls back losers by following prevLSN chains, writing a **Compensation Log Record (CLR)** for each undone action; a CLR's **undoNextLSN** pointer skips already-undone work, so CLRs are never undone and repeated crashes during recovery make **bounded, monotone progress** (undo never grows the log unboundedly).

**Mechanism B — Fuzzy checkpoints.** Rather than quiescing the system, an ARIES **fuzzy checkpoint** writes begin/end-checkpoint records containing snapshots of the DPT and ATT without flushing dirty pages; the **master record** points at the latest checkpoint. Recovery cost is bounded by how far recLSNs trail the checkpoint, so background writers advance the "oldest dirty page" watermark. (PostgreSQL by contrast uses flush-based checkpoints spread over `checkpoint_completion_target`, with redo starting at the checkpoint's redo pointer.)

**Mechanism C — Shadow paging.** The System R research prototype's alternative to in-place update: maintain **current and shadow page tables**; updates copy-on-write pages and install them in the current page table, and commit atomically swaps the root pointer to make the current table the new shadow. Recovery is trivial (the shadow is a consistent state), no redo/undo needed — but it destroys physical clustering, makes page-table maintenance and garbage collection expensive, and complicates concurrent transactions, which is why ARIES-style WAL won. Its intellectual descendants are **copy-on-write/append-only B-trees** (LMDB, ZFS, Btrfs) where the atomic root swap *is* the commit.

**Mechanism D — LSM/WAL replay recovery.** Log-structured engines (RocksDB, Cassandra) recover by (a) replaying the WAL into fresh memtables up to the last synced record, discarding torn tail records via per-record **CRC checksums**, and (b) reconstructing the SSTable level structure from the **MANIFEST** (a log of version edits, itself atomically advanced via the CURRENT file). Because SSTables are **immutable**, there is no in-place page state to repair — recovery reduces to log replay plus metadata reconstruction, with the doublewrite/full-page-write problem of §1 eliminated by construction.

---

## Synthesis

A single thread ties these areas together: **durability and ordering are both achieved by turning state changes into logs**. WAL (§1) makes single-node commits a log append; ARIES (§8) exploits that log with repeating-history redo and CLR-protected undo; LSM trees (§3) promote the log to the primary storage structure, while B+trees (§4) keep in-place pages but log their SMOs as nested top actions. MVCC (§2) replaces locks with versioned history ordered by transaction IDs or timestamps — which, in distributed settings, must come from logical or hybrid clocks (§6). Atomic commitment across shards (§5) and replica agreement (§7) are then the distributed analogues of the local commit record: 2PC's forced prepare record generalizes the WAL rule across machines, quorum intersection generalizes "the commit record is on stable storage," and consensus-hardened commit (Paxos Commit, Spanner) closes 2PC's blocking window exactly as flexible quorums (FPaxos) tune the availability/latency tradeoff of that replication.

Answer: The complete technical brief above covers all eight areas with ≥3 named mechanisms each — (1) WAL: ARIES physiological logging/LSNs, steal/no-force policies, group commit, doublewrite buffer & full_page_writes; (2) MVCC: PostgreSQL xmin/xmax+VACUUM, InnoDB undo-based read views, SSI with SIREAD locks, Hekaton MVOCC; (3) LSM: memtable/SSTable flush pipeline, leveled vs. size-tiered vs. universal compaction, Bloom filters & fence pointers, tombstones/RUM tradeoffs; (4) B+trees: split/merge/redistribution, latch crabbing & optimistic lock coupling, Lehman–Yao B-link trees, logged SMOs & next-key locking; (5) 2PC: prepare/commit with the blocking problem, presumed abort/commit, 3PC, Paxos Commit/Spanner 2PC-over-Paxos; (6) logical clocks: Lamport clocks, vector clocks/DVVs, HLC, TrueTime; (7) quorums: R+W>N with sloppy quorums & hinted handoff, Gifford weighted voting, grid/tree quorums, Flexible Paxos; (8) crash recovery: ARIES analysis/redo/undo with CLRs, fuzzy checkpoints (DPT/ATT), shadow paging, and LSM WAL/MANIFEST replay.

# Write-Ahead Logging (WAL)

## 1. ARIES physiological logging, LSNs, and the WAL rule

**Log record granularity.** ARIES (Algorithms for Recovery and Isolation Exploiting Semantics, Mohan et al. 1992) uses *physiological logging*: physical to a page, logical within the page. A record identifies the page ID and describes the operation (e.g., "insert tuple into slot on page P") rather than a byte-level before/after image of the whole page. This is a compromise between pure physical logging (large records, but idempotent redo) and pure logical logging (compact, but hard to redo after partial writes). Each update record carries undo information (before-image or logical undo action) and redo information (after-image or logical redo action).

**LSNs.** Every log record is assigned a monotonically increasing *Log Sequence Number*, typically the record's byte offset in the log so the record is addressable directly. Key LSN variables:

- **pageLSN**: stored in each data page header, the LSN of the last log record that modified that page. This is the linchpin of redo idempotence: redo applies a record to a page only if `record.LSN > pageLSN`.
- **prevLSN**: in each log record, pointer to the previous record of the same transaction, forming a per-transaction backward chain used by undo.
- **flushedLSN**: in memory, the LSN up to which the log has been durably forced to stable storage.
- **recLSN** (recovery LSN): per dirty page, the LSN of the first record that dirtied the page since it was last flushed; lower-bounds where redo must begin for that page.
- **lastLSN**: per transaction, the most recent record written by that transaction.
- **undoNextLSN**: in compensation log records, see recovery section.

**The WAL rule (two protocols).**
1. *Undo rule (the WAL rule proper)*: before a dirty page is written to disk, all log records up to and including that page's pageLSN must be flushed. Enforced as: flush log until `flushedLSN ≥ pageLSN` before evicting the page. This guarantees undo information exists for any uncommitted change that reaches disk.
2. *Commit rule (force-log-at-commit)*: a transaction is not acknowledged as committed until all its log records, including the commit record, are on stable storage (durability).

## 2. Steal / no-force buffer management policies

Two orthogonal axes of buffer-pool policy determine what recovery must do:

- **Steal vs. no-steal**: may the buffer manager write a page dirtied by an *uncommitted* transaction to disk (e.g., to evict it)? Steal = yes. Steal requires **undo** logging, because aborted/uncommitted changes may be on disk at crash time.
- **Force vs. no-force**: must all pages dirtied by a transaction be flushed to disk *at commit*? Force = yes. No-force requires **redo** logging, because committed changes may exist only in the log at crash time.

Policy matrix:

| Policy | Undo needed | Redo needed | Performance |
|---|---|---|---|
| No-steal / force | no | no | worst (random I/O at commit, pinned buffers) |
| No-steal / no-force | no | yes | buffer pool capped by uncommitted working set |
| Steal / force | yes | no | commit-time flush storms |
| Steal / no-force | yes | yes | best; what ARIES assumes |

ARIES is explicitly designed for **steal/no-force**, trading recovery complexity (both redo and undo passes) for normal-case throughput: commits require only a sequential log force, and the buffer manager evicts freely.

## 3. Group commit

With force-log-at-commit, each commit nominally costs one synchronous log I/O (an `fsync`/`fdatasync` or FUA write). *Group commit* amortizes this: the log manager delays the flush briefly so that log records from many concurrently committing transactions accumulate in the log buffer, then forces them with a **single** sequential write. One fsync durably commits the whole batch; all waiting transactions are then acknowledged together.

- Trade-off: slightly higher commit latency for each transaction vs. dramatically higher commit throughput (fsyncs/second is the bottleneck, not bytes).
- Implementations: PostgreSQL `commit_delay`/`commit_siblings` plus its WAL-insertion lock design; MySQL/InnoDB binary-log group commit (the leader/follower, multi-stage commit queue introduced in 5.6+); most engines make batching adaptive rather than timer-only (flush fires when the previous flush completes, naturally batching whatever arrived meanwhile).
- Related relaxations: *asynchronous commit* (PostgreSQL `synchronous_commit = off`, InnoDB `innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit = 0/2`) acknowledges before the force, bounding potential loss of recent commits but never sacrificing consistency, since the WAL rule itself is still honored.

## 4. Fuzzy checkpoints

A checkpoint bounds how much log recovery must scan. Naive (*sharp*) checkpoints quiesce all activity and flush every dirty page, which stalls the system. ARIES uses **fuzzy checkpoints**, taken concurrently with normal processing and flushing nothing synchronously:

1. Write a `begin_checkpoint` record.
2. Write an `end_checkpoint` record containing snapshots of the **Dirty Page Table (DPT)** — page ID plus recLSN for each dirty buffer page — and the **Transaction Table / Active Transaction Table (ATT)** — each active transaction's status and lastLSN.
3. Atomically record the begin_checkpoint LSN in a known location (the *master record*, e.g., ARIES's master log record, PostgreSQL's `pg_control`).

The checkpoint is "fuzzy" because the tables are captured while updates continue; correctness comes from the analysis pass reconstructing exact state from the checkpoint plus the subsequent log. Redo must start not at the checkpoint but at **min(recLSN) over the checkpointed DPT**, since dirty pages may predate the checkpoint. Background writers continuously flush dirty pages to advance min(recLSN) and allow log truncation. PostgreSQL's checkpointer with `checkpoint_completion_target` (spreading page flushes over the interval) and InnoDB's fuzzy checkpointing driven by flushing the oldest-modification pages from the flush list are production instances of the same idea.

## 5. Torn-page protection

A "torn page" (partial write) occurs when a crash interrupts a multi-sector page write: the OS/disk atomically writes 512 B–4 KB sectors, but database pages are 4–16 KB, so a page can land half-old/half-new. Physiological redo *cannot repair this*: redo logic reads the pageLSN and assumes the page is internally consistent, which a torn page is not.

- **InnoDB doublewrite buffer**: before writing dirty pages to their final tablespace locations, InnoDB first writes them sequentially to a dedicated doublewrite area (historically 2 MB in the system tablespace, separate `#ib_16384_*.dblwr` files since MySQL 8.0.20), fsyncs, then writes the pages in place. On recovery, any torn page in the tablespace (detected via per-page checksum) is restored from its intact copy in the doublewrite buffer, after which normal redo applies. Cost ≈ 2× page-write volume but mostly sequential; can be disabled on filesystems with atomic page writes (e.g., ZFS, or 16K-atomic-write capable storage).
- **PostgreSQL full_page_writes (FPW / full-page images, FPIs)**: the first time a page is modified after each checkpoint, PostgreSQL logs the *entire page image* into WAL instead of only the delta. During redo, that FPI is restored wholesale, obliterating any torn state; subsequent delta records then apply on top. Cost is WAL inflation right after checkpoints (mitigated by `wal_compression`); benefit is no separate doublewrite structure.
- **Checksum-based detection as the trigger**: both schemes rely on detecting corruption — InnoDB page checksums, PostgreSQL `data_checksums` / the per-WAL-record CRC. SQL Server's equivalents are `PAGE_VERIFY = CHECKSUM` (detection) with repair from log/backup, and its log records similarly carry parity checks.
- Alternative: **copy-on-write / log-structured storage** (LMDB's shadowed B-tree, ZFS/Btrfs CoW, SQLite in WAL mode appending whole pages) sidesteps torn writes by never overwriting a live page in place.

---

# Crash Recovery

## 1. ARIES three-pass recovery

Guiding principle: **repeating history**. On restart, ARIES first re-establishes the exact pre-crash state — including the effects of *uncommitted* transactions — and only then rolls back losers. This is what lets it support fine-grained (record-level) locking, partial rollbacks via savepoints, and logical undo of index operations, which earlier schemes that redid only winners could not.

**Pass 1 — Analysis.** Scan forward from the begin_checkpoint of the last complete checkpoint (located via the master record):

- Rebuild the **ATT**: add a transaction on seeing its first record; mark it committed/ended on commit/end records; at pass end, remaining entries are *loser transactions* needing undo, each with its lastLSN as the starting point.
- Rebuild the **DPT**: on an update record for page P not in the DPT, insert P with recLSN = that record's LSN. The result is a conservative superset of pages possibly dirty at crash.
- Outputs: the loser set, and **redoLSN = min(recLSN) across the DPT**, where redo begins.

**Pass 2 — Redo (repeating history).** Scan forward from redoLSN, applying *every* redoable record — winners' and losers' alike, including CLRs. For each record touching page P, apply it only if **all three** hold: P is in the DPT; record.LSN ≥ P's recLSN; and after reading the page, record.LSN > pageLSN. The pageLSN comparison makes redo idempotent across repeated crashes during recovery. After redo, the database state equals the instant of the crash.

**Pass 3 — Undo.** Roll back all losers in a single backward scan: repeatedly pick the record with the **largest LSN among all losers' undoNext pointers**, undo it, and follow prevLSN. For every undone update, write a **Compensation Log Record (CLR)**:

- A CLR is **redo-only** — it is never itself undone. This bounds undo work: even with crashes during recovery, each original update is undone at most once, and the log consumed by rollback is bounded (no cascading compensation of compensations, unlike schemes that logged undos as ordinary updates).
- Each CLR carries **undoNextLSN** = the prevLSN of the record just compensated, i.e., the next record still needing undo. If a crash interrupts undo, the next recovery's redo pass replays the CLRs (re-applying the compensations), and undo resumes directly at undoNextLSN, skipping already-undone work. This same machinery implements normal-runtime rollback and savepoint-based partial rollback.
- When a loser is fully undone, write an end record and drop it from the ATT.

**Supporting features**: nested top actions (for structure modifications like B-tree splits that must persist even if the enclosing transaction aborts — implemented with a dummy CLR whose undoNextLSN jumps over the action), logical undo for index records (the key may have moved pages since the original insert), and recovery independence per page.

## 2. Shadow paging (System R)

The historical alternative to WAL for atomicity, used by IBM System R's storage layer (and surviving in LMDB and SQLite's rollback-journal-era design lineage):

- The database is reached through a **page table** (page map). Two versions exist: the **shadow** version — the last committed, consistent state, never modified in place — and the **current** version being updated.
- An update copies the target page to a free location, modifies the copy, and updates the *current* page table to point at it; the shadow page table still points at the old page.
- **Commit** = flush all current pages and the current page table, then **atomically swing one root pointer** (a single-sector write) from the shadow table to the current table. The old shadow pages become garbage to reclaim.
- **Crash recovery is trivial**: the root still points at the shadow state, so restart simply discards the orphaned current pages. No redo, no undo, no log analysis.

**Why ARIES won**: commit cost is proportional to the page table (no-force-like benefits lost at scale); data becomes fragmented because logical page adjacency is destroyed by relocation, ruining sequential scans; garbage collection of superseded pages is needed; and crucially, a single shadow root supports only **one writer** (or page-level concurrency at best) — concurrent fine-grained transactions require combining shadowing with logging anyway, which System R in fact did (shadow paging plus a log for transaction undo). Copy-on-write B-trees (LMDB, CouchDB, ZFS) are the modern descendants, accepting the single-writer model in exchange for instant recovery and MVCC-style readers.

## 3. Checkpoint-based recovery structures: DPT and ATT

The two tables are the hinge between checkpointing and recovery, worth treating as mechanisms in their own right:

- **Dirty Page Table (DPT)**: runtime structure in the buffer manager mapping page ID → recLSN, where recLSN is set when a clean page is first dirtied (the LSN of the dirtying record, or the current end of log) and the entry is removed when the page is flushed. Checkpointed copy: lets analysis start from the checkpoint rather than the log's beginning, and its min(recLSN) defines both the redo start point and the **log truncation point** — log before min(recLSN of DPT, lastLSN of oldest active transaction) may be archived/recycled. During redo, the DPT acts as a filter so pages known to have been flushed are never even read.
- **Active Transaction Table (ATT / transaction table)**: maps transaction ID → (state: in-progress / committing / candidate-for-undo, lastLSN, undoNextLSN). Checkpointed copy seeds analysis; final version drives the undo pass and, in distributed settings, identifies **in-doubt transactions** (prepared under two-phase commit) that must be preserved, not rolled back, pending the coordinator's verdict.
- **Master record / control file**: the fixed-location anchor (ARIES master record, PostgreSQL `pg_control` with its redo pointer, InnoDB's checkpoint fields in the log file header, written to two alternating slots for atomicity) from which recovery finds the last complete checkpoint. Without it, recovery would need a scan from the log's origin.

**End-to-end flow tying it together**: fuzzy checkpoint persists DPT+ATT snapshots → crash → analysis reconstructs exact DPT/ATT from checkpoint + log tail → redo repeats history from min(recLSN), gated per page by pageLSN → undo rolls back ATT losers via prevLSN chains, writing redo-only CLRs with undoNextLSN → torn pages encountered along the way have already been healed before/during redo by doublewrite restoration or full-page-image replay, which is why physiological redo can trust pageLSN at all.

---

**Summary of findings.** For WAL I covered five mechanisms: ARIES physiological logging with the LSN family and both halves of the WAL rule, the steal/no-force policy matrix and why ARIES targets steal + no-force, group commit with PostgreSQL and InnoDB implementations, fuzzy checkpoints capturing DPT/ATT snapshots, and torn-page protection via InnoDB's doublewrite buffer versus PostgreSQL full-page writes plus the copy-on-write alternative. For crash recovery I covered three mechanisms: ARIES's analysis/redo/undo passes with repeating history, CLRs, and undoNextLSN; System R shadow paging and why logging displaced it; and the DPT/ATT/master-record structures that connect checkpoints to recovery. The closing flow paragraph shows the dependency ordering a synthesizer can reuse: torn-page repair must precede redo, redo precedes undo, and log truncation is governed by min(recLSN) and the oldest active transaction.

# MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control)

## PostgreSQL: in-place version chains with xmin/xmax

PostgreSQL stores all tuple versions directly in the heap. Each tuple header carries system columns: `xmin` (XID of the inserting transaction), `xmax` (XID of the deleting/updating transaction, or 0/invalid if live), `ctid` (physical location, also used as a forward pointer to the newer version after an UPDATE), plus `cmin`/`cmax` (command IDs for intra-transaction visibility) and infomask hint bits (`HEAP_XMIN_COMMITTED`, `HEAP_XMAX_COMMITTED`, etc.) that cache commit status to avoid repeated `pg_xact` (CLOG) lookups.

**UPDATE is delete + insert.** An UPDATE sets `xmax` on the old version and inserts a new version with `xmin` = updater's XID. The old tuple's `ctid` points to the successor, forming a forward-growing version chain (newest versions are reached by following `ctid`; indexes point at the chain, and readers chase it). HOT (Heap-Only Tuple) updates avoid new index entries when no indexed column changed and the new version fits on the same page: the chain is followed via the page-internal HOT chain and the index entry continues to reference the root line pointer.

**Snapshots.** A snapshot is the triple (`xmin`, `xmax`, `xip[]`): the oldest in-progress XID, the first unassigned XID, and the list of XIDs in progress at snapshot time. Tuple visibility: a tuple is visible iff its inserting transaction committed and is "in the past" of the snapshot (XID < snapshot xmax and not in `xip`), and its `xmax` is either invalid, aborted, or not yet visible under the same test. READ COMMITTED takes a new snapshot per statement; REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE take one snapshot at the first statement and keep it.

**VACUUM.** Because dead versions accumulate in the heap, PostgreSQL needs garbage collection. VACUUM removes tuple versions dead to all transactions (older than the global `xmin` horizon / `GlobalVisState`), reclaims line pointers, updates the free space map and visibility map (all-visible/all-frozen bits enable index-only scans and vacuum skipping), and **freezes** old tuples by setting `HEAP_XMIN_FROZEN`, which is essential to prevent 32-bit XID wraparound. Autovacuum triggers on dead-tuple thresholds and on `autovacuum_freeze_max_age` (anti-wraparound vacuum). Long-running transactions hold back the xmin horizon, causing bloat because dead tuples can't be reclaimed. Index entries pointing to dead tuples are removed in the vacuum's index pass; `VACUUM FULL` rewrites the table.

## InnoDB and Oracle: undo-based version reconstruction

These systems update **in place** and reconstruct old versions on demand from undo.

**InnoDB.** Each clustered-index record carries hidden columns `DB_TRX_ID` (last modifying transaction) and `DB_ROLL_PTR` (pointer into the rollback segment's undo log record). To read an old version, InnoDB follows the roll pointer and applies undo records backward until it reaches a version visible to the reader's **read view**. A read view records the low/high water marks (`up_limit_id`, `low_limit_id`) and the set of active transaction IDs (`m_ids`) at creation; a record version is visible if its `DB_TRX_ID` is below the low mark, or below the high mark and not in the active set, or equals the reader's own ID. REPEATABLE READ creates the read view at the first consistent read; READ COMMITTED creates one per statement. Secondary index records carry no trx info; InnoDB checks the page's max TRX ID and falls back to the clustered index for visibility. **Purge** threads garbage-collect undo records no longer needed by any read view and physically remove delete-marked records; a long-lived read view causes **history list length** growth (undo bloat), the analogue of PostgreSQL bloat. Note InnoDB's RR is snapshot-based for plain reads but uses **current reads** (locking reads with next-key locks) for `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` and DML, which is why it is not true snapshot isolation.

**Oracle.** Functionally similar: changes generate undo in undo tablespaces; read consistency is enforced at the **SCN** (System Change Number) level. A query reads blocks as of its snapshot SCN; if a block has been modified since (checked via ITLs — Interested Transaction List slots in the block header), Oracle clones the block and rolls it back by applying undo to produce a **consistent read (CR) block**. If the needed undo has been overwritten (undo_retention exceeded), the query fails with **ORA-01555 "snapshot too old"** — the classic failure mode of bounded version storage. Statement-level consistency is the default; SERIALIZABLE sets the snapshot SCN at transaction start. Block cleanout (delayed logging of commit status in ITLs) parallels PostgreSQL hint bits.

## Snapshot Isolation anomalies and SSI

Snapshot Isolation (SI) prevents dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, phantoms, and lost updates (via **first-committer-wins** / first-updater-wins write-write conflict detection), but is not serializable. The characteristic anomaly is **write skew**: two transactions read overlapping data, each writes a disjoint item, and both commit; e.g., two doctors each read "two doctors on call" and each take themselves off call, violating the constraint "at least one on call." A related anomaly is **read-only transaction anomaly** (Fekete et al. 2004), where even a read-only transaction can observe a non-serializable state.

**Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI)** (Cahill, Röhm, Fekete 2008; implemented in PostgreSQL 9.1, Ports & Grittner 2012) runs transactions under SI and tracks **rw-antidependencies** (rw-conflicts: T1 reads a version that T2 later overwrites, so T1 → T2 in the serialization graph). Theory (Fekete et al.): every SI anomaly cycle contains two **consecutive rw-antidependency edges**, with the "pivot" transaction having both an incoming and outgoing rw-edge. SSI aborts a transaction when such a **dangerous structure** (T0 —rw→ T1 —rw→ T2, with T2 committing first) is detected — a conservative test with false positives but no false negatives. PostgreSQL implements this with **SIREAD locks**: non-blocking predicate markers taken on tuples, pages, or whole relations read by serializable transactions (with lock-granularity promotion under memory pressure, increasing false-positive aborts). SIREAD locks block nothing; they exist only to detect rw-conflicts, and must be retained after commit until all concurrent serializable transactions finish. Failed transactions get `serialization_failure` (SQLSTATE 40001) and must be retried. Read-only transactions can run safely via `SERIALIZABLE READ ONLY DEFERRABLE`, which waits for a provably safe snapshot and then needs no SIREAD tracking.

## Hekaton: timestamp-ordered, latch-free MVCC

Microsoft Hekaton (SQL Server In-Memory OLTP; Larson et al. 2011, Diaconu et al. 2013) is a fully in-memory, lock-free MVCC engine. Each version carries a **Begin** and **End timestamp** defining its validity interval. A transaction gets a **read time** (begin timestamp) and reads the version whose [Begin, End) interval contains it — reads never block. On update, a writer installs its transaction ID in the old version's End field and the new version's Begin field, acting as an exclusive claim; a second writer encountering a transaction ID there aborts (first-writer-wins, eager write-write conflict detection). At commit the transaction acquires a monotonically increasing **commit timestamp** and rewrites its transaction IDs with it; commit dependencies allow speculative reads of uncommitted versions, resolved at commit.

For full serializability Hekaton uses **optimistic validation** instead of SSI: at commit it (1) **rereads** the read set to verify each version is still visible as of the commit timestamp (detects non-repeatable reads), and (2) **rescans** index ranges recorded during execution to detect phantoms. Repeatable Read requires only the reread; Snapshot Isolation requires no validation. All index structures (Bw-tree, lock-free hash) and version management are **latch-free**, using compare-and-swap only; garbage collection is cooperative and parallel, removing versions whose End timestamp precedes the oldest active transaction's read time. Durability is via a log of committed transactions plus checkpoints; indexes are not logged and are rebuilt on recovery.

**Contrast summary:** PostgreSQL = old versions in the main heap, cleaned by VACUUM, readers never reconstruct; InnoDB/Oracle = newest version in place, old versions reconstructed backward from undo, cleaned by purge/undo retention; Hekaton = all versions first-class in memory with timestamp intervals, latch-free, validation-based serializability.

# B+tree concurrency and maintenance

## Split, merge, redistribution

**Split.** Inserting into a full leaf (capacity 2d entries) splits it into two nodes of ~d entries each; a **separator key** (copy of the new right sibling's low key, since B+tree leaves hold all keys) is inserted into the parent. Parent overflow splits propagate recursively; splitting the root grows the tree by one level, which is how a B+tree gains height. Internal-node splits **move** the median key up rather than copying it. Many systems split unevenly for append patterns (e.g., rightmost-leaf splits leave the left node full — "90/10" or leaf-split-right optimization).

**Delete: merge and redistribution.** When a node underflows (< d entries), the textbook algorithm first tries **redistribution (key rotation/borrowing)** from an adjacent sibling through the parent — moving entries and updating the separator key — and otherwise **merges (coalesces)** the node with a sibling, deleting the separator from the parent; parent underflow propagates upward, and a root with one child is removed, shrinking the tree. In practice most engines (including PostgreSQL and historically InnoDB's simpler policy) use **lazy deletion**: pages are never actively rebalanced; a page is reclaimed only when it becomes completely **empty**, at which point it is unlinked and recycled (PostgreSQL marks it half-dead, then deleted, and recycles it only after no concurrent scan can still land on it — governed by a safe-xid/RecentGlobalXmin check, now the `btpo_xact`/safe horizon). This trades space for drastically simpler concurrency, justified empirically by Johnson & Shasha's "free-at-empty" analysis.

## Latch crabbing and optimistic lock coupling

Standard terminology distinguishes **latches** (short-term physical consistency, no deadlock detection) from **locks** (logical, transaction-duration, deadlock-managed).

**Latch coupling / crabbing.** Descend holding at most two latches: latch child, verify, release parent. Readers take shared latches. For writers, **pessimistic crabbing** holds exclusive latches on the whole path until reaching a **safe node** (one that cannot split on insert — not full — or cannot underflow on delete — more than minimum occupancy); once a safe child is latched, all ancestor latches are released, since an SMO cannot propagate past it. The **optimistic variant** descends with shared latches assuming the leaf-level operation won't propagate, takes exclusive only on the leaf, and **restarts in pessimistic mode** if the leaf turns out unsafe. This is the Bayer–Schkolnick (1977) family of protocols.

**Optimistic Lock Coupling (OLC)** (Leis et al. 2016/2019): each node has a versioned latch (version counter + lock bit). Readers take no latches at all; they read the version, read the node, and **re-validate** the version afterward (restarting on mismatch, i.e., if a writer intervened), coupling validations parent-to-child like latch coupling but lock-free for reads. Writers acquire the latch, which increments the version on release. OLC gives near-lock-free read scalability on multicore with minimal code change versus true lock-free designs like the **Bw-tree** (Levandoski et al.), which avoids latches entirely via delta records and a mapping table with CAS installation.

## Lehman–Yao B-link trees

Lehman & Yao (1981) allow safe concurrent access with at most one latch held at a time (in the original paper, no read latches at all). Two structural additions: every node has a **right-sibling link** and a **high key** (upper bound on keys in the node). A split is performed **right-to-left in two phases**: (1) create the new right sibling, move the upper half of entries, set links/high keys — the tree is already consistent and searchable at this point via the sibling link; (2) later (possibly by another operation) insert the separator into the parent. A reader that descends using a stale parent and lands on a node whose high key is less than its search key simply **moves right** along the sibling link. This decouples the split from the parent update, eliminating the need for latch coupling during descent: an in-progress split is indistinguishable from a completed split whose parent pointer hasn't been followed. Deletion was not handled by Lehman–Yao; **Lanin & Shasha (1986)** added symmetric deletion with left-links/outlinks, and PostgreSQL's nbtree is explicitly a Lehman–Yao implementation (with latches on individual pages, high keys, move-right logic, and the page-deletion algorithm using half-dead pages and sibling-link repair).

## Structure modification operations (SMOs) and their logging

An **SMO** is any multi-page structural change: split, merge, page deletion, root growth/shrink. The core problem is atomicity and recoverability of a multi-page, multi-log-record change interleaved with independent user transactions.

**ARIES/IM** (Mohan & Levine 1992) treats an SMO as a **nested top action (NTA)**: the sequence of log records for the SMO is terminated by a **dummy CLR** (compensation log record) whose UndoNxtLSN points before the SMO's first record. If the enclosing transaction later aborts, undo skips over the SMO — the split stays in place (it's a physical reorganization, logically neutral), and only the logical key insert is undone. If the system crashes **mid-SMO**, redo replays the logged portion and undo (via the normal CLR chain, since no dummy CLR was written) rolls the partial SMO back, restoring structural consistency. A tree latch / SMO bit serializes conflicting SMOs and lets in-flight operations detect and wait out an incomplete SMO.

Alternatives: **System-transaction** approach (e.g., SQL Server, and as described by Graefe): the SMO runs as a separate short **system transaction** that commits immediately (needing no flush, since it changes no logical content), independent of the user transaction; the user's key insert then proceeds in the user transaction. PostgreSQL instead makes **each atomic step of an SMO a single WAL record** (a split is one WAL record covering both pages; the parent insert is a separate record) and, on crash between steps, finishes the incomplete split **lazily on next visit** (detected via the B-link invariants and a page flag, `P_INCOMPLETE_SPLIT`), which is only possible because Lehman–Yao trees are search-consistent between steps. Shadow-paging/copy-on-write trees (LMDB, append-only B-trees) sidestep SMO logging entirely by never updating pages in place.

Physiological logging (ARIES) is standard for the page content itself: redo is physical per page, undo is logical (undo a key insert by deleting the key wherever it now lives, since splits may have moved it — this is why index undo must re-traverse).

## Key-range / next-key locking

These are **locks**, not latches: they enforce serializability (phantom protection) over a key range without predicate-lock generality, by exploiting B+tree key order. Locking the gap requires an existing key to attach the lock to — the **next key**.

**ARIES/KVL** (Mohan 1990) and **ARIES/IM**: an operation on key k locks k and, for inserts/deletes and range-scan boundaries, the **next key** in order, so the lock on key k' covers the open interval (previous-key, k'] — the record plus the gap before it. A range scan locks each key read plus the key just past the range end, preventing phantom inserts into any scanned gap. Deletes lock the next key so the gap left by the deleted key stays protected. **Instant duration** locks are used for insert's next-key check (test for conflict, don't hold).

**InnoDB terminology:** a **record lock** covers the index record only; a **gap lock** covers the open interval before a record; a **next-key lock** is record + preceding gap (conceptually (prev, rec]); an **insert intention lock** is a gap-lock variant taken before inserting, compatible with other insert intentions in the same gap but blocked by gap/next-key locks — this is the phantom-prevention mechanism under REPEATABLE READ for locking reads. The pseudo-record **supremum** anchors locks on the gap above the largest key. Gap locks are purely inhibitive (they only block inserts) and are mostly disabled at READ COMMITTED.

**Graefe's refinement (key-range locking with separate lock modes):** locking a key and its gap as one unit over-locks; hierarchical/multi-granularity modes (e.g., RangeS-S, RangeS-U, RangeI-N, RangeX-X in SQL Server; Graefe's "key and gap as separate resources" design) let a transaction lock the key but not the gap or vice versa, increasing concurrency. Fence keys and ghost records interact here: **ghost (pseudo-deleted) records** let a delete be a logical flag flip — the ghost's key remains as a lock anchor and the physical removal is a later system transaction, which simplifies both key-range locking and SMO-free deletion.

---

**Key cross-cutting points for synthesis:** (1) MVCC removes read-write blocking but moves the cost to version storage and GC (VACUUM vs. purge vs. cooperative GC) and, for serializability, to conflict tracking (SIREAD rw-antidependency detection vs. Hekaton read-set/scan-set revalidation vs. InnoDB falling back to next-key locking). (2) In B+trees, latches protect physical structure while key-range locks protect logical ranges; B-link side pointers and NTA/system-transaction logging both exist to make multi-page SMOs appear atomic to concurrent traversals and to recovery, respectively.

response.content:
# LSM-Tree Storage Engines: Deep Technical Coverage

## 1. Core Architecture: Memtable, WAL, SSTables, Flush

### Write path
A Log-Structured Merge-tree (O'Neil et al., 1996) buffers writes in memory and defers/batches disk I/O so that all on-disk writes are sequential.

1. **Write-Ahead Log (WAL)**: Every mutation (put/delete/merge) is first appended to a sequential, append-only WAL (RocksDB: `.log` file; Cassandra: commit log) for durability. Group commit batches multiple writers' fsyncs. Each record carries a monotonically increasing **sequence number** (LSN), which is the basis for MVCC snapshot isolation in RocksDB (snapshots pin a sequence number).
2. **Memtable**: The mutation is then applied to an in-memory, sorted, mutable structure — typically a **skip list** (RocksDB default, supports concurrent inserts), though red-black trees, tries (Cassandra 4+ trie memtables), or hash-skiplists are used. Point lookups and range scans hit the memtable first.
3. **Immutable memtable & flush**: When the memtable reaches a size threshold (`write_buffer_size`), it is atomically swapped for a fresh memtable and marked **immutable**. A background flush thread serializes it into a sorted run on disk — an **SSTable (Sorted String Table)** — at **Level 0** (RocksDB/LevelDB). After the flush is durable, the corresponding WAL segment can be truncated/recycled. If flushes/compactions fall behind, the engine applies **write stalls** or write stops (RocksDB: triggers on L0 file count, pending compaction bytes, number of immutable memtables) — this is backpressure to bound space and read amplification.

### SSTable internal format
An SSTable is an immutable, sorted sequence of key-value entries, organized as:

- **Data blocks** (typically 4–64 KB), each holding sorted KV pairs with **prefix compression** (restart points every N entries to allow intra-block binary search).
- **Index block**: a sparse index mapping the last key of each data block to its offset — these per-block index entries are the **fence pointers**. RocksDB supports partitioned (two-level) indexes for huge files.
- **Filter block**: per-file (or per-block / partitioned) **Bloom filter**.
- **Metaindex + footer**: locates index/filter blocks; footer contains magic number and format version.
- Each file records its key range [smallest, largest] and sequence-number range in the **manifest/version** metadata (LevelDB `MANIFEST`, a log of `VersionEdit`s; Cassandra keeps per-SSTable metadata/Statistics components). Readers operate on an immutable **Version** (snapshot of the file set) via reference counting, so compaction can install new versions atomically.

### Read path
Point lookup for key *k*:
1. Probe active memtable, then immutable memtable(s).
2. Search L0 files **newest-to-oldest** (L0 files have overlapping key ranges, so all whose range covers *k* must be checked).
3. For each sorted level L1…Ln, binary-search the level's file metadata to find the single file (levels are non-overlapping) whose range covers *k*; consult its Bloom filter; if positive, binary-search the index block (fence pointers) to pick one data block; read and search that block.
4. Return the newest version ≤ the read snapshot's sequence number; a tombstone terminates the search with "not found."

Range scans use a **merging iterator** (heap-based k-way merge) over memtables and all relevant runs, deduplicating by sequence number.

---

## 2. Compaction Strategies

Compaction merges sorted runs: it sort-merges SSTables, drops overwritten versions and expired tombstones, and rewrites the result. The strategy determines the shape of the tree and the write/read/space amplification profile.

### 2.1 Leveled compaction (LevelDB, RocksDB `kCompactionStyleLevel`, Cassandra LCS)
- Levels L1…Ln each hold a **single sorted run**: a set of SSTables with **disjoint key ranges** within the level. Level capacities grow geometrically by a **fanout/size ratio T** (default 10): `max_bytes_for_level_base` for L1, ×10 per subsequent level.
- L0 is special: flushed memtables land there as whole files with **overlapping** ranges (it's a tiered buffer).
- When level Li exceeds its target size, a compaction picks one file (plus any overlapping files) from Li, finds all overlapping files in Li+1, merges them, and writes new non-overlapping files into Li+1. File selection heuristics: round-robin cursor (LevelDB), most-overwritten/oldest, or RocksDB's `kMinOverlappingRatio`.
- RocksDB refinements: **dynamic level sizing** (`level_compaction_dynamic_level_bytes`, sizing levels relative to the last level to bound space amplification at ~1/T ≈ 10%), **intra-L0 compaction**, **subcompactions** (parallelizing one compaction by key range), and **trivial move** (when no overlap, just re-link the file).

**Properties**: at most one run per level ⇒ read amplification is O(number of levels) ≈ O(log_T N) probes (plus L0 files); space amplification bounded near 1 + 1/T because at most ~1/T of data is stale; but **write amplification is high**: each entry is rewritten up to ~T times per level, giving total WA ≈ O(T · log_T N) — in practice 10–30× for RocksDB defaults.

### 2.2 Size-tiered compaction (Cassandra STCS, HBase, Lucene-style; RocksDB "tiering")
- Runs are grouped into **tiers/buckets of similar size**. When a tier accumulates `min_threshold` (default 4) similarly-sized SSTables, they are merged into one larger SSTable in the next tier. Each entry is merged roughly once per tier.
- Within a "level" there can be **up to T overlapping runs**, so reads must check all of them.

**Properties**: **write amplification is low**: each entry is copied ~once per tier ⇒ WA ≈ O(log_T N). But **read amplification** is O(T · log_T N) run probes, and **space amplification can reach O(T)** — transiently ~2× during a big merge (need room for inputs + output), and stale versions of a key can exist in every run of every tier. STCS also suffers with update-heavy workloads because old versions linger in large, rarely-compacted SSTables (Cassandra mitigates with "single-SSTable compactions" based on droppable-tombstone ratio, and offers **TWCS** — time-window compaction — for TTL'd time-series data, which buckets SSTables by time window and lets whole expired SSTables be dropped).

### 2.3 Universal compaction (RocksDB `kCompactionStyleUniversal`)
RocksDB's generalization of size-tiered compaction operating on a totally ordered sequence of sorted runs (newest to oldest, where a run is an L0 file or an entire level). Compactions pick a contiguous prefix/suffix of runs, triggered by three conditions evaluated in precedence order:
1. **Space amplification trigger** (`max_size_amplification_percent`): if estimated size-amp = (sum of all runs except the last) / (size of last run) exceeds the threshold, compact **everything** into one run (full compaction).
2. **Size-ratio trigger** (`size_ratio`): merge consecutive runs while each candidate run's size is within `(1 + size_ratio/100)` of the accumulated size of the newer runs — this merges similarly-sized runs, i.e., classic tiering behavior.
3. **Run-count trigger** (`level0_file_num_compaction_trigger`): if the number of sorted runs exceeds the limit, merge enough newest runs to get under it.

Universal trades toward low write amplification (tiering-like, ≈ O(log_T N) or tunable) at the cost of read amplification proportional to the run count and **temporary 2× space amplification** during full compactions. It's the standard choice for bulk-ingest and write-dominated workloads; many deployments ingest under universal then switch to leveled.

### 2.4 Hybrids & variants (for completeness)
- **Lazy leveling** (Dayan & Idreos, *Dostoevsky*, 2018): tiering at all levels except the largest, which is leveled — captures tiering's write cost while bounding space-amp and point-read cost like leveling. **Fluid LSM-tree / Wacky** generalizes with per-level run-count knobs (K for inner levels, Z for the last level), making leveling, tiering, and lazy leveling points in one continuum.
- **Partitioned tiering** (ScyllaDB ICS, RocksDB universal with subcompactions) to cut the transient space overhead of monolithic tiered merges.
- **FIFO compaction** (RocksDB): pure TTL-based file dropping for caches.

---

## 3. Auxiliary Structures

### 3.1 Bloom filters
- A per-SSTable (or per-partition) **Bloom filter** is a probabilistic set-membership structure: m bits, k hash functions; false-positive rate ε ≈ (1 − e^(−kn/m))^k, minimized at k = (m/n)·ln 2, giving ε ≈ 0.6185^(m/n). Typical sizing: 10 bits/key ⇒ ε ≈ 1%.
- Purpose: on a point lookup, skip any run whose filter reports "absent," so a key is read from disk only from runs that (probabilistically) contain it. **No false negatives**; false positives cost one wasted index+block probe.
- Implementation details: RocksDB uses **full filters** (one filter per file, checked before the index) or **partitioned filters**; **block-based filters** are deprecated. RocksDB's modern filter is a cache-local **Ribbon filter** option (smaller than Bloom for the same ε, at higher construction CPU) and uses double hashing to simulate k hashes from 2. **Prefix Bloom filters** accelerate prefix seeks. Cassandra sizes filters via `bloom_filter_fp_chance` (default 0.01 STCS, 0.1 LCS — coarser for LCS because fewer runs must be probed).
- **Bloom filters do not help range queries** (no membership test over an interval); that motivates fence pointers and range-filter structures (SuRF, Rosetta, prefix filters).

### 3.2 Fence pointers
- **Fence pointers** are the sparse in-memory/index-block entries recording the first (or last) key of each data block (and, at coarser granularity, the min/max key of each SSTable held in the manifest/version metadata). They let a lookup binary-search to the exact block, so a filter-positive point read costs **one** block I/O, and a range scan seeks directly to the first qualifying block in each run.
- Standard LSM cost accounting assumes fence pointers + filters are memory-resident; refinements include **partitioned/two-level indexes** (RocksDB) for memory pressure, and compressed fence pointers (e.g., FAST/Hollow variants in research literature).

### 3.3 Block cache & compression
(Adjacent but standard): uncompressed block cache (RocksDB LRU/Clock, Cassandra chunk cache), per-level compression (e.g., no compression for L0–L1, LZ4 mid-levels, ZSTD bottom level), and dictionary compression for the last level.

---

## 4. Tombstones and Deletes

- A delete is a **write**: it inserts a **tombstone** (deletion marker) with its own sequence number/timestamp. The tombstone shadows older versions during reads and merges.
- A tombstone **cannot be dropped** until it has been compacted together with (or provably below) **all older versions of the key** — in leveled compaction, only when the compaction output is the **bottommost level** containing that key range (LevelDB/RocksDB check `IsBaseLevelForKey` / bottommost-level status); otherwise an older version in a deeper run would "resurrect."
- **Cassandra specifics**: tombstones are retained for at least `gc_grace_seconds` (default 10 days) before being purgeable, to allow anti-entropy repair to propagate the delete to all replicas; purging early risks **zombie/resurrected data** if a replica missed the delete. Cassandra also has **range tombstones** (deleting a clustering range/partition) and emits `TombstoneOverwhelmingException`/warnings when scans read too many tombstones.
- **Pathologies**: tombstone pileup makes reads scan-and-discard large numbers of dead cells (classic "queue anti-pattern"); tombstones inflate space until purged (space amplification); and non-existent-key deletes still write tombstones. Mitigations: RocksDB `DeleteRange` (native range tombstones), `SingleDelete` (droppable on meeting exactly one put), **compaction-on-tombstone-density triggers** (RocksDB `CompactOnDeletionCollector`, Cassandra `tombstone_threshold` single-SSTable compactions), and TTL-based whole-file drops (TWCS/FIFO).

---

## 5. Amplification Tradeoffs: RUM, Monkey, Dostoevsky

### 5.1 The three amplifications
For N total entries, memtable/buffer of B entries, fanout T, L ≈ log_T(N/B) levels:

| Metric | Definition | Leveled | Tiered |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Write amplification (WA)** | bytes written to storage / bytes of user writes (includes WAL + flush + every compaction rewrite) | O(T · L) — each entry rewritten up to T−1 times per level | O(L) — ~once per level |
| **Read amplification (RA)** | I/Os (or runs probed) per lookup | point: O(L) runs, ~1 with filters (≈ 1 + L·ε expected I/Os); range: O(L) seeks | point: O(T·L) runs; range: O(T·L) seeks |
| **Space amplification (SA)** | physical bytes / logical live bytes | ≈ 1 + 1/T (≈1.1 with dynamic leveling) | up to O(T); ≥ 2× transient during full merges |

**RUM conjecture** (Athanassoulis et al., 2016): for Read, Update (write), and Memory/space overheads, an access method can optimize at most two at the expense of the third — a three-way tradeoff, not a free lunch. LSM compaction strategies are points on this surface: leveling favors R and M at cost of U; tiering favors U at cost of R and M; B-trees favor R at cost of U and M; and auxiliary memory (filters, indexes) buys R with M.

### 5.2 Monkey (Dayan, Athanassoulis, Idreos — SIGMOD 2017)
Monkey showed the **standard uniform allocation of Bloom-filter bits per key across all levels is suboptimal**. Insight: expected wasted I/O per lookup = Σ over runs of that run's false-positive rate, while filter memory cost per run scales with the run's entry count — but FPR improves exponentially in bits/key. Since deeper levels hold exponentially more entries (T× per level), a bit spent on a small upper-level run buys the same FPR reduction far more cheaply.

- **Result**: the optimal allocation gives **more bits per key to smaller/upper levels** and exponentially fewer to deeper levels — the FPRs should **increase geometrically with depth** (and the largest level may get no filter at all, since a true point read must end there anyway). 
- This reduces expected point-lookup cost from O(L · e^(−M/N)) to **O(e^(−M/N))** for the same total filter memory M — asymptotically removing the dependence on the number of levels — or equivalently saves ~an order of magnitude of filter memory at equal lookup cost.
- Monkey additionally exposes (T, buffer size, memory split between filters and cache) as a **self-tuning design space**, navigating the RUM tradeoff analytically per workload. Follow-ups: **Dostoevsky** (lazy leveling + Fluid LSM, removing superfluous merging for entries that only ever get point-read or that never reach the last level) and **Wacky/endure**-style design continuums.

### 5.3 Practical tuning levers (mapping theory → knobs)
- **Fanout T** (`max_bytes_for_level_multiplier`, STCS `min_threshold`): larger T ⇒ fewer levels (better reads/space in leveling) but more rewriting per level in leveling; in tiering, larger T ⇒ fewer merges (better writes) but more runs to probe.
- **Buffer size B** (`write_buffer_size`, memtable count): larger ⇒ fewer, larger flushes, fewer levels, lower WA; costs memory and recovery time.
- **Filter bits/key** and allocation (Monkey): trades memory vs. point-read I/O.
- **Compaction style per workload**: write-heavy/ingest ⇒ universal/tiered; read-heavy or space-constrained ⇒ leveled; TTL time-series ⇒ TWCS/FIFO; mixed ⇒ lazy-leveling-style hybrids.
- **Key-value separation** (WiscKey lineage; RocksDB **BlobDB**, Titan, Badger): store large values in a value log and only keys+pointers in the LSM, slashing WA for large values at the cost of extra indirection on reads, garbage collection of the value log, and worse range-scan locality.

### 5.4 Secondary effects worth naming
- **Compaction debt and write stalls**: sustained ingest beyond compaction bandwidth grows L0/pending-compaction bytes until stall triggers fire; throughput becomes compaction-bound.
- **SSD interaction**: host-level WA multiplies with device-level (FTL) WA; LSM sequential writes are FTL-friendly, but high host WA burns endurance — a core motivation for tiering/universal and KV separation.
- **Cache pollution**: compaction rewrites invalidate block-cache entries for rewritten blocks (mitigations: compaction-aware caching, `compaction_readahead`, pinning L0/metadata blocks).

**Bottom line**: an LSM-tree converts random writes into sequential I/O via the memtable+WAL+flush pipeline and immutable SSTables; the compaction policy (leveled vs. size-tiered vs. universal/hybrid) selects a point on the RUM surface trading write amplification against read and space amplification; Bloom filters and fence pointers buy back point-read cost with memory (optimally allocated per Monkey); and tombstones make deletes writes whose reclamation is governed by compaction reaching the bottommost level (plus `gc_grace_seconds` in replicated systems).
